Friend,
Adam Hamilton’s campaign started with a simple idea: Kansans deserve a leader who listens to them. Our representatives should be fighting to end the chaos and corruption in Washington. Roger Marshall isn’t getting the job done.
When Marshall is not in Washington cutting SNAP benefits for kids and slashing Medicaid, he spends much of his time at his second home in Florida — _1,500 miles away from the people he represents!_ **And what’s worse? It’s been over 500 days since he held a public town hall in Kansas.**
**That’s not acceptable. You can’t drive up costs for Kansas families and then hide out at your home on the water. It’s time we held our leaders accountable.[If you’re ready to retire Sen. | | Dear Peter,
Thank you for your support of [this historic Kshama for Congress campaign](https://us.list-manage.com/SGVhKXO8IX8?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15). **We won the highest ever vote, by far, for a revolutionary socialist candidate for Congress, with 17.3 percent of voters in the district choosing Kshama.** We achieved this despite the myriad obstacles and maneuvering by the Democratic and Republican parties.
This shows the growing anger at the two parties for their endless attacks on the conditions of working people, and for their full-throated support of horrific imperialist wars and the US-backed Israeli genocide of the Palestinian people. And it shows the growing desire for political leaders who are unambiguous in their allegiances to the interests of working-class and oppressed people, and who are fighting for bold demands like taxing the rich to fund free healthcare for all and putting in place a full arms embargo against Israel.
Through this campaign, thanks to your efforts and the efforts of thousands of others, we spread the incredible history of how Kshama used her position on the Seattle City Council to win major victories for working people. **For a decade in that position, Kshama led militant movements and went to war against the political establishment to win the highest minimum wage in the nation, the Amazon Tax, landmark renters' rights, and much more.** We need more political leaders who are willing to take this approach if we are going to have a shot at turning the tide against the billionaires and their political servants in the US and around the world.
We saw during this Congressional campaign the poisonous role of the left and labor gatekeepers. The Democratic Socialists of America, the so-called "progressive" Democratic elected officials, and many prominent left media figures refused to support Kshama. The business unionist labor leadership across all the major unions lined up to support warmongering billionaire-backed Democrat Adam Smith. As working-class anger pushes these left and labor gatekeepers into higher prominence, they will be tested. name: Gina Hinojosa
subject: Greg Abbott has failed our public schools.
body:
Under Abbott’s leadership, nearly 4 out of 10 public schools in Texas are falling behind.
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter,
Texas recently released its latest academic accountability rating, and the verdict is in: public school performance is falling flat.
**Of more than 9,000 campuses across the state, nearly 40% scored a C, D, or an F – 4 out of 10 Texas schools are failing or barely scraping by under Greg Abbott's watch.**
And even more troubling — the schools receiving failing grades at disproportionate rates are **predominantly low-income, Hispanic and Black communities.**
**The same communities** that are already underfunded and overlooked. The same communities that trigger state takeovers, with entire districts being stripped of local control while wealthier schools continue to receive higher ratings and more resources.
These ratings unjustly punish the schools that need the most help instead of providing them with the support they actually deserve. And yet, Abbott and his administration keep pushing forward as if nothing is wrong.
Our students and teachers deserve better. And our communities deserve a governor who will _actually_ invest in public education instead of letting schools fail.
**I'm running to change that — to fully fund our public schools, to support our teachers, and to make sure every child in Texas, regardless of their zip code, background, or socioeconomic status — has access to a quality education.**
**[So, will you chip in today to help us build the campaign we need to defeat Greg Abbott and give Texas public schools the leadership they deserve?](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/1356?c0=em_ms_gh_20260905_4_schools.x-gkrs&refcode=em20260905-2024&t=1&akid=2024%2E299639%2EPp_QiI)**

Let's build a Texas where every school and student succeeds.
Thank you,
Gina Hinojosa

name: Mark Kelly
subject: This was not the plan:
body:
Team, when
Gabby and I first agreed that I would run for Senate back in 2019, we knew
things would change. We know more than most how public service can change
your life.

But I’ve got to tell you, I never intended for things to end up like this.
All I wanted to do was keep serving my country, the same way I have since
I was sworn in to the U.S. Navy.

I know that service comes with risk, sure. But I didn’t set out to be
threatened with a court-martial by the Secretary of Defense, or to have
the President of the United States calling for my execution.

Look, I don’t want you to worry about me. I’ve been through a lot in my
life, and things like this don’t intimidate me all that much.

I do worry that Trump might succeed at intimidating others, though. Like
people just beginning to get involved, or thinking about joining a
peaceful demonstration, or speaking out at a town hall. I worry Trump and
his cronies are trying to scare people out of resisting him.

But then I see millions of people meeting this moment with the courage and
resolve it demands of them. People like my friend Chris Pappas. It makes
me hopeful, sure. But more than that, it makes me incredibly proud.

We’re ready to fight like hell to save our democracy. If you’re with me,
please:

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260905_4.DCgGNF&refcode=em20260905-4&t=1001&akid=8722%2E582294%2E1k6cbc ]Split a donation between me and Chris Pappas. $5 or
anything you can afford.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260905_4.DCgGNF&amount=5&refcode=em20260905-4&t=1020&akid=8722%2E582294%2E1k6cbc ]Donate $5 »

Thanks so much,

Mark

On January 5th, a White House deputy chief of staff named Stephen Miller went on CNN and, in the middle of getting testy with Jake Tapper about Greenland, said the quiet part out loud about Venezuela.
Tapper was pushing him on something simple: two days earlier, U.S. forces had raided Caracas and flown Nicolas Maduro out of his own country in shackles. Why, Tapper asked, wasn't the administration calling for an election? Miller didn't really answer that question. He answered a different one.
"The United States is using its military to secure our interests unapologetically in our hemisphere," he said. "We're a superpower, and under President Trump, we are going to conduct ourselves as a superpower." Then came the line that mattered: it would be absurd, he said, to let a country in our own backyard sell its resources to our adversaries **" but not to us."**
Four words. Read them again. He didn't say Venezuela's oil belongs to Venezuelans, and that no outside power should be allowed to loot it. He didn't say we can't tolerate a hostile military foothold ninety minutes from Florida. He said the unacceptable thing was that the oil might go to someone else _and not to us._
Hold that sentence up against what happened next.
Eight months later, **the United States government holds a 35% equity stake in a private oil company that has just been handed hundred-year concessions to seventeen Venezuelan oil fields holding roughly 65 billion barrels of crude** -- about a fifth of the country's entire reserves. DC gets guaranteed access to 20% of everything Venezuela's state oil company produces, at cost. It gets first right of refusal on the rest. It gets veto power over the company's board.
The White House itself is calling this "U.S. majority control" and describing it, without apparent embarrassment, as a **restoration of American dominance** in the hemisphere for the century ahead.
So maybe we should take Miller seriously. Not as a gaffe. As a doctrine statement.
This essay is not about Maduro, per se. Nor Trump, for that matter. It's about something underneath this whole conflagration: **what does a powerful country actually acquire by being powerful?**
And the answer this administration has given, in word and now in a signed hundred-year contract, is: **more than it should.**

## First: The strategic case is real.
The United States has an actual, serious, legitimate interest in secure, geographically nearby, heavy crude oil supply.
_Especially_ since we started bombing Iran.
Since late February, the U.S. and Israel have been functionally at war with Iran, and Iran responded by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz -- a passage that, before the war, carried something like a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade and a fifth of its liquefied natural gas. Ships are still hitting mines there this week. American forces are still trading strikes with Iranian ones this week.
If your job is thinking about where America's fuel comes from twenty years from now, the idea of leaning harder on a hemisphere we don't have to create a war zone to reach is not crazy. It's due diligence.
Venezuela, specifically, makes an unusual amount of sense for this. It sits a short Caribbean hop from the Gulf Coast. Its crude is heavy and sour -- not the light, sweet oil that gushes out of American shale, but exactly the grade that a huge slice of Gulf Coast refining capacity was purpose-built decades ago to process. **A real U.S. -Venezuela energy partnership, honestly negotiated, could be enormously good for both countries:** American investment and refining capacity meeting Venezuelan reserves and desperate need for capital, jobs, and reconstruction.
Fine. Makes sense. Let's write that down, underline it, and then notice what it **doesn 't** require.
None of it requires an invasion. None of it turns an American strategic preference into a Venezuelan legal obligation. None of it requires abducting the sitting head of state of a sovereign country and flying him to Brooklyn in chains. **Wanting a thing badly, even wanting it for good reasons, is not the same as being entitled to it.**
That's the whole essay, compressed into one sentence: **interest is not title.**
I can want your oil. I can offer to buy it, invest in it, build pipelines and refineries for you around it, and make you an offer so good you'd be foolish to say no.
**What I cannot do is make the leap of moral logic from "I need it" to "you owe it to me."** That's precisely the leap Stephen Miller hid inside four words on CNN.

## Monroe, before he became an excuse
The doctrine Miller is purporting to update didn't start out this way.
In 1823, the United States was a minor power making a defensive request: **European empires, please don 't come back and recolonize the newly independent republics of this hemisphere.** That's genuinely modest as imperial doctrines go. Buried inside it is a principle worth keeping -- that distant, powerful empires shouldn't treat weaker American states as property to be redistributed among themselves.
The mutation started, fittingly, over Venezuelan debt. In 1902, European creditor powers blockaded Venezuelan ports to collect on defaulted loans. Theodore Roosevelt's answer wasn't "Europe may not coerce Latin America." It was "Europe may not coerce Latin America, because _we_ will do the coercing." **The Roosevelt Corollary claimed for the United States an "international police power" throughout the hemisphere**, and it opened two decades of occupations -- Cuba, Nicaragua, Haiti, the Dominican Republic.
That's where it went toxic: Monroe said 'outsiders don't get to dominate this hemisphere.' Roosevelt quietly rewrote that into 'America gets to intervene throughout it.'
The current administration has now taken the next step, and it isn't shy about it. Its November 2025 National Security Strategy explicitly declared a "Trump Corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine, promising to keep the hemisphere "free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets" and to reassert American preeminence over it. Roosevelt's corollary was about excluding rival empires. This one adds a possessive Miller supplied for free on cable news: not just that Venezuela shouldn't arm itself against us, but that its resources shouldn't go to _them_ instead of _us_.
Monroe: outsiders don't get to run this hemisphere.
Roosevelt: therefore we get to police it.
Trump and Miller: therefore we get to decide who its resources belong to.
Each step feels like a small addition. Stacked up, they add up to something Monroe would not recognize, and no person with basic moral conscience should support.
## What actually happened, in order
In December 2025, the administration ordered a "total and complete" naval blockade of sanctioned tankers moving in and out of Venezuela, backed by what Trump called the largest naval force ever assembled in the region, and in the same breath demanded Venezuela return America's "Oil, Land, and other Assets." (Notably - and we'll get into this - according to Venezuela's constitution, their oil is a sovereign public asset that belongs to the Venezuelan people.) U.S. forces began boarding and seizing tankers, including at least one carrying Venezuelan crude toward China.
On January 3rd, U.S. special operations forces attacked Caracas and captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, flying them to a Navy ship and then to New York to face narco-trafficking charges. Trump said the U.S. would "run" the country until a transition could be arranged. Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal, rather than declaring the presidency vacant and triggering the election the constitution calls for in that circumstance, declared Maduro merely and forcibly _absent_ -- and installed his own vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, as interim president two days later.
Two days after that came the CNN interview. Within the week, Washington and Caracas had agreed to move tens of millions of barrels of Venezuelan crude through a U.S.-controlled sales structure. On January 9th, Trump signed an executive order **asserting U.S. Treasury custody over the resulting oil revenue** -- an order that, does, at least on the face of it, explicitly state the money remains Venezuela's sovereign property, just held and disbursed at Washington's discretion. Sanctions began easing. Venezuela's petroleum laws were rewritten under Rodriguez to give operators more autonomy and easier access to foreign capital, on the same days Washington relaxed the sanctions squeezing the industry.
By July, the _Financial Times_ estimated **DC had collected on the order of $13 billion from Venezuelan oil sales, with only partial public accounting for where it went.**
Then, on August 31st, the White House announced the deal that makes this whole essay necessary: **the Pentagon 's Office of Strategic Capital -- a body that, weeks earlier, had publicly stated it does not take equity stakes in private companies -- took a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, the company that just received hundred-year rights to seventeen oil fields and 65 billion barrels.** (It's worth noting that the current US Deputy Secretary of Defense, Stephen Feinberg, is a venture capitalist and Wall Street billionaire who has publicly treated US government defense/war contracting as his personal fiefdom, and secured astonishing contracts for his "former" firm's companies. I wrote about him [earlier](https://substack.com/redirect/e0c749b6-50eb-4b99-9f0e-6586b4382580?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).) Venezuela's National Assembly, dominated by Rodriguez's own party, ratified this arrangement days later.
Then, Reuters reported just this week: **the Venezuelan businessman at the center of that deal, Alejandro Betancourt, had until recently been a target of a U.S. money-laundering investigation tied to funds embezzled from Venezuela 's state oil company.** His lawyer says the allegations have been examined for years across multiple jurisdictions and never produced charges, and that's a fair thing to note. It's also fair to note that he reportedly assisted U.S. authorities in the run-up to Maduro's capture, and that the investigation into him appears to have gone quiet around the same time. Make of that what you will.
There you go, folks: doctrine, blockade, invasion, custody of the money, rewritten law, and finally a durable ownership stake. Every step both increased American leverage and moved it one degree closer to the oil itself.

## Three legal systems agree: this is not ok.
### International law
The UN Charter's starting proposition, forged out of two world wars, **is that states are legally equal regardless of how powerful or how badly governed they are**. Article 2(4) bars the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence. The exceptions are narrow and few:
a. Security Council authorization, or
b. self-defense under Article 51 following an actual armed attack.
**There was no Security Council authorization for the attack that seized Maduro on January 3rd.** There is no publicly documented Venezuelan armed attack on the United States that would trigger Article 51.
A domestic criminal indictment -- leaving aside the question of its legitimacy -- gives American courts jurisdiction to put on trial someone who ends up in an American courtroom. It does not, under international law, license flying special operations forces into a foreign capital to put him there.
That's not a hippie reading -- it's why the UN Secretary-General said publicly that he was "deeply concerned" the operation hadn't respected international law, and why the blockade that preceded it maps almost exactly onto the UN General Assembly's own definition of aggression, which explicitly names blockading another state's ports as one of its clearest examples.
### American law
The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to declare war, and the War Powers Resolution says that putting U.S. forces into hostilities is supposed to reflect Congress's judgment as well as the president's.
Congress never declared war on Venezuela. It never passed an authorization for the use of military force there. The operation wasn't a response to an attack on American soil or American forces.
The administration's position -- that a short, decapitating strike doesn't rise to a "war" requiring prior authorization -- is a real legal theory, and presidents of both parties have leaned on versions of it before.
But Congress clearly didn't think the question was settled. The Senate voted 52-47 to advance a war powers resolution days after the raid, then killed it in a 51-50 procedural vote after the White House spent a week working on two wavering Republicans, with the Vice President flown in to break the tie.
The House defeated a similar measure two weeks later on a dead-even 215-215 vote that Republican leaders held open for twenty extra minutes to get one more member to the floor.
Congress didn't stop it after the fact -- barely. But still: **that is not the same thing as Congress authorizing it.**

### Venezuelan law
This is the part almost no one in US media has covered, and it's worth serious consideration.
Venezuela's constitution has plenty to say about all of this. Article 302 reserves the petroleum industry to the state as a matter of national interest. Article 303 requires the state to retain PDVSA itself (Venezuela's state-owned oil company). Article 150 requires National Assembly approval for contracts of national public interest with foreign states -- which the Assembly has, in fact, now given. (Reasonable people may note the remarkable application of coercive pressure by external forces shaping the conditions under which that consent was granted.)
But approval by whom, on whose authority? Maduro's own Supreme Tribunal ruled his removal a _temporary_ absence, not a permanent one, and under Article 234 that framework caps a vice president's caretaker role at 90 days, extendable once by the Assembly for another 90. **Rodr iguez's initial 90 days expired in early April with no public Assembly vote to extend it. The outer 180-day limit came and went by early July. No extension vote. No presidential election**, though Article 233 says a _permanent_ vacancy in a president's first four years is supposed to trigger one within 30 days. Rodriguez simply kept governing, and two months after that constitutional clock ran out, _her government signed a hundred-year contract over a fifth of the nation 's oil reserves._
I'm not saying the concessions are automatically void, or that Venezuelan courts and the Assembly can't retroactively bless what's happened -- they plainly intend to, and probably will, for as long as this government holds power.
What I am saying is that a future, differently constituted Venezuelan government has a serious, textually grounded argument that an interim administration whose own constitutional clock had already expired -- ergo, who should no longer be serving in office, since elections were constitutionally required to be held -- lacked the authority to bind the country for a century.
**If you want a hundred-year oil contract, the first thing you need is a government whose legitimacy can survive more than six months.** This one, on its own country's terms, currently cannot.

## Consent under a gun
Suppose you set all three of those legal problems aside. Suppose Rodriguez's government signs, the Assembly ratifies, and Venezuelan courts eventually bless the whole structure. There's still a harder question sitting underneath the paperwork: **what is consent worth when the party asking for it also controls the coercive environment the "yes" gets produced in?**
The 1969 Vienna Convention has a name for this. Article 52 says **a treaty procured by the unlawful threat or use of force is void.** I'm not claiming that single clause dissolves a three-layer commercial arrangement involving a private company and private equity terms -- it doesn't work that cleanly, and Reuters' own reporting treats the governmental agreement, the Venezuelan concessions, and the corporate equity deal as legally distinct layers.
But the governmental layer is exactly the scenario the clause was written for:
One state invades another,
removes its government,
keeps a military and economic chokehold on it,
tells the world out loud that the target now needs its permission to trade -- and then
negotiates a resource deal with the successor authority that situation produced, and
calls the result consensual.
**Really now.**
Try the universality test, which is the single most useful tool in this whole argument: **would you accept this reasoning from anyone else?** Imagine China invading a mineral-rich neighbor, capturing its president, propping up his own deputy as "interim president," and then announcing a hundred-year mining concession with a Chinese government equity stake, on the grounds that the interim government approved it.
Nobody serious would call that a legitimate contract.
Therefore, it doesn't become one just because DC did it instead of Beijing.
## Interest, right, sovereignty, duty
Let's break this down. There are four fundamental concepts we're working with here.
(And I'm sick and tired of real and important words being turned into a funhouse mirror of meaning, just so powerful interests can do whatever they want, sabotage our clarity of mind, and keep us from fighting back because we can't even talk about things clearly.
So. Definitions.)
An _**interest**_ is something that benefits you. America has real interests in Venezuelan oil, in keeping hostile militaries out of this hemisphere, and in a stable, diversified energy supply.
A _**right**_ is something you're entitled to demand. Wanting Venezuelan oil, even wanting it for excellent reasons, **does not create an American right to it**.
_Sovereignty_ is the principle that it's Venezuelans -- not Americans, Russians, or Chinese -- who get to decide what happens to Venezuela's resources and government, within the bounds of international law and the rights of Venezuelans themselves.
And _duty_ is what power is supposed to cost you. The more capability a state has to simply take what it wants, the less credible its excuse for just-taking-it becomes. Power is _supposed_ to be ennobling.

There's an old line, popularized of all places by a comic-book hero, that has outlived the comic: **with great power comes great responsibility.** It sounds almost too simple to belong in a foreign policy essay, and that's exactly why it belongs here.
What I hear underneath Miller's four words, and underneath a hundred-year contract signed with a government whose own legal clock had run out, is closer to the inverse: **with great power comes great impunity.** "_We can, therefore we may and we will, and if you don 't like it -- who's going to stop us?_"
That might be an accurate description of what power enables you to do. **It is not a theory of law; it is definitely not a theory of moral goodness, equal dignity, or mutual respect; and it is a genuinely dangerous theory of leadership,** because it only works for exactly as long as you're the strongest party in the room, and no country stays that forever.
An angry man filled with lust may be capable of overpowering a woman.
That does not make rape OK.
## The best version of their case -- and why it still isn't enough
Let's steelman this: Maduro ran an authoritarian, corrupt government that stole an election and impoverished its own people. Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence in the hemisphere is a long-term security concern. Venezuela's oil industry has been starved of capital and expertise for two decades and desperately needs both. American investment could genuinely help rebuild it. If Rodriguez's government and the National Assembly want to strike this bargain, maybe that's Venezuela choosing the least-bad option available to it.
I take all of that seriously. **My answer is: then make that case to a government whose authority isn 't itself in dispute, and make an offer good enough that Venezuelans choose it freely.** Offer the investment, the technology, the market access, the debt relief. Compete for that relationship the way you'd want a suitor to compete for something that's actually yours to give away.
If getting the deal required warships, a military abduction, an economic chokehold, and a government installed by the same power now buying its resources -- that isn't evidence the deal is a good one. It's evidence that, were it offered honestly, it might not have been accepted at all.
## The superpower I actually want
None of this is an argument for American weakness. On the contrary. It's an argument for America to be **stronger** , in the specific way that matters most: discipline. Integrity. Self-restraint. Responsibility.
**I want America to be powerful enough to keep its word.** To live up to its ideals. To honor its treaties and uphold its responsibilities. To be a force for good in the world. To provide help in times of disaster, and support recovery with dignity instead of possessive self-interest. To negotiate with respect, to act with integrity, and to genuinely participate in building a better, stronger, more peaceful world, jointly with the many other people and countries with whom we share this planet.
In my ideal world, America keeps sea lanes open; deters attacks on its people without attacking anyone else; secures its (green!) energy future; invests in climate justice, resilience, and adaptation; and negotiates genuinely excellent deals. It's strong enough that other countries choose to trade with it because the offer is good, not because refusing carries an economic or military price.
This means America **must** be strong enough to exercise restraint -- because restraint only means something when you could dominate someone and choose not to.
Nearly every empire in history has managed to make weaker countries obey it for a while. That was never the hard test. The hard test, the one very few powers have ever passed, is whether you can hold overwhelming power and not become a bully with it.

## "But Not To Us."
Stephen Miller probably thought he was making a throwaway point on cable news. Read against everything that followed -- the blockade, the raid, the custody of the money, the rewritten petroleum law, the equity stake, the hundred-year lease on a fifth of a country's oil -- it reads less like a gaffe and more like the whole doctrine, stated nakedly before anyone had bothered to dress it up.
Venezuela has the right to sell its oil to the United States. It has the right to sell it to China. It has the right to make a bad deal and the right to make a brilliant one. Its government has duties to its own people, and its people have rights against their government that no foreign power gets to override on their behalf. America can compete, invest, negotiate, and protect its own interests with everything it's got. What it can't do -- what no country gets to do, no matter how big its navy is -- is decide that its need for something someone else owns, makes that something rightfully its own.
We tell children that with great power comes great responsibility. It might be superpowers that need the reminder most. Because the alternative -- great power, great impunity, and everyone else can shove it -- doesn't stop with Venezuela. It ends in a world where every strong state takes what it can get away with, every weak one arms itself against the possibility, and sovereignty means nothing more than whatever the strongest military in the room says it means.
We built something better than that world once, out of the wreckage of two world wars. It would be a genuine shame to trade that hard-won architecture of geopolitical responsibility for 65 billion barrels.

On Venezuela, oil, and what great powers are actually allowed to do. | | | Sep 5 | | | | | | | | | | | | On January 5th, a White House deputy chief of staff named Stephen Miller went on CNN and, in the middle of getting testy with Jake Tapper about Greenland, said the quiet part out loud about Venezuela. Tapper was pushing him on something simple: two days earlier, U.S. forces had raided Caracas and flown Nicolas Maduro out of his own country in shackles. Why, Tapper asked, wasn't the administration calling for an election? Miller didn't really answer that question. He answered a different one. "The United States is using its military to secure our interests unapologetically in our hemisphere," he said. "We're a superpower, and under President Trump, we are going to conduct ourselves as a superpower." Then came the line that mattered: it would be absurd, he said, to let a country in our own backyard sell its resources to our adversaries " but not to us." Four words. Read them again. He didn't say Venezuela's oil belongs to Venezuelans, and that no outside power should be allowed to loot it. He didn't say we can't tolerate a hostile military foothold ninety minutes from Florida. He said the unacceptable thing was that the oil might go to someone else and not to us. Hold that sentence up against what happened next. Eight months later, the United States government holds a 35% equity stake in a private oil company that has just been handed hundred-year concessions to seventeen Venezuelan oil fields holding roughly 65 billion barrels of crude -- about a fifth of the country's entire reserves. DC gets guaranteed access to 20% of everything Venezuela's state oil company produces, at cost. It gets first right of refusal on the rest. It gets veto power over the company's board. The White House itself is calling this "U.S. majority control" and describing it, without apparent embarrassment, as a restoration of American dominance in the hemisphere for the century ahead. So maybe we should take Miller seriously. Not as a gaffe. As a doctrine statement. This essay is not about Maduro, per se. Nor Trump, for that matter. It's about something underneath this whole conflagration: what does a powerful country actually acquire by being powerful? And the answer this administration has given, in word and now in a signed hundred-year contract, is: more than it should. | | ---|---|--- First: The strategic case is real. The United States has an actual, serious, legitimate interest in secure, geographically nearby, heavy crude oil supply. Especially since we started bombing Iran. Since late February, the U.S. and Israel have been functionally at war with Iran, and Iran responded by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz -- a passage that, before the war, carried something like a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade and a fifth of its liquefied natural gas. Ships are still hitting mines there this week. American forces are still trading strikes with Iranian ones this week. If your job is thinking about where America's fuel comes from twenty years from now, the idea of leaning harder on a hemisphere we don't have to create a war zone to reach is not crazy. It's due diligence. Venezuela, specifically, makes an unusual amount of sense for this. It sits a short Caribbean hop from the Gulf Coast. Its crude is heavy and sour -- not the light, sweet oil that gushes out of American shale, but exactly the grade that a huge slice of Gulf Coast refining capacity was purpose-built decades ago to process. A real U.S. -Venezuela energy partnership, honestly negotiated, could be enormously good for both countries: American investment and refining capacity meeting Venezuelan reserves and desperate need for capital, jobs, and reconstruction. Fine. Makes sense. Let's write that down, underline it, and then notice what it doesn 't require. None of it requires an invasion. None of it turns an American strategic preference into a Venezuelan legal obligation. None of it requires abducting the sitting head of state of a sovereign country and flying him to Brooklyn in chains. Wanting a thing badly, even wanting it for good reasons, is not the same as being entitled to it. That's the whole essay, compressed into one sentence: interest is not title. I can want your oil. I can offer to buy it, invest in it, build pipelines and refineries for you around it, and make you an offer so good you'd be foolish to say no. What I cannot do is make the leap of moral logic from "I need it" to "you owe it to me." That's precisely the leap Stephen Miller hid inside four words on CNN. Monroe, before he became an excuse The doctrine Miller is purporting to update didn't start out this way. In 1823, the United States was a minor power making a defensive request: European empires, please don 't come back and recolonize the newly independent republics of this hemisphere. That's genuinely modest as imperial doctrines go. Buried inside it is a principle worth keeping -- that distant, powerful empires shouldn't treat weaker American states as property to be redistributed among themselves. The mutation started, fittingly, over Venezuelan debt. In 1902, European creditor powers blockaded Venezuelan ports to collect on defaulted loans. Theodore Roosevelt's answer wasn't "Europe may not coerce Latin America." It was "Europe may not coerce Latin America, because we will do the coercing." The Roosevelt Corollary claimed for the United States an "international police power" throughout the hemisphere, and it opened two decades of occupations -- Cuba, Nicaragua, Haiti, the Dominican Republic. That's where it went toxic: Monroe said 'outsiders don't get to dominate this hemisphere.' Roosevelt quietly rewrote that into 'America gets to intervene throughout it.' The current administration has now taken the next step, and it isn't shy about it. Its November 2025 National Security Strategy explicitly declared a "Trump Corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine, promising to keep the hemisphere "free of hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets" and to reassert American preeminence over it. Roosevelt's corollary was about excluding rival empires. This one adds a possessive Miller supplied for free on cable news: not just that Venezuela shouldn't arm itself against us, but that its resources shouldn't go to them instead of us. Monroe: outsiders don't get to run this hemisphere. Roosevelt: therefore we get to police it. Trump and Miller: therefore we get to decide who its resources belong to. Each step feels like a small addition. Stacked up, they add up to something Monroe would not recognize, and no person with basic moral conscience should support. What actually happened, in order In December 2025, the administration ordered a "total and complete" naval blockade of sanctioned tankers moving in and out of Venezuela, backed by what Trump called the largest naval force ever assembled in the region, and in the same breath demanded Venezuela return America's "Oil, Land, and other Assets." (Notably - and we'll get into this - according to Venezuela's constitution, their oil is a sovereign public asset that belongs to the Venezuelan people.) U.S. forces began boarding and seizing tankers, including at least one carrying Venezuelan crude toward China. On January 3rd, U.S. special operations forces attacked Caracas and captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, flying them to a Navy ship and then to New York to face narco-trafficking charges. Trump said the U.S. would "run" the country until a transition could be arranged. Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal, rather than declaring the presidency vacant and triggering the election the constitution calls for in that circumstance, declared Maduro merely and forcibly absent -- and installed his own vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, as interim president two days later. Two days after that came the CNN interview. Within the week, Washington and Caracas had agreed to move tens of millions of barrels of Venezuelan crude through a U.S.-controlled sales structure. On January 9th, Trump signed an executive order asserting U.S. Treasury custody over the resulting oil revenue -- an order that, does, at least on the face of it, explicitly state the money remains Venezuela's sovereign property, just held and disbursed at Washington's discretion. Sanctions began easing. Venezuela's petroleum laws were rewritten under Rodriguez to give operators more autonomy and easier access to foreign capital, on the same days Washington relaxed the sanctions squeezing the industry. By July, the Financial Times estimated DC had collected on the order of $13 billion from Venezuelan oil sales, with only partial public accounting for where it went. Then, on August 31st, the White House announced the deal that makes this whole essay necessary: the Pentagon 's Office of Strategic Capital -- a body that, weeks earlier, had publicly stated it does not take equity stakes in private companies -- took a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, the company that just received hundred-year rights to seventeen oil fields and 65 billion barrels. (It's worth noting that the current US Deputy Secretary of Defense, Stephen Feinberg, is a venture capitalist and Wall Street billionaire who has publicly treated US government defense/war contracting as his personal fiefdom, and secured astonishing contracts for his "former" firm's companies. I wrote about him .) Venezuela's National Assembly, dominated by Rodriguez's own party, ratified this arrangement days later. Then, Reuters reported just this week: the Venezuelan businessman at the center of that deal, Alejandro Betancourt, had until recently been a target of a U.S. money-laundering investigation tied to funds embezzled from Venezuela 's state oil company. His lawyer says the allegations have been examined for years across multiple jurisdictions and never produced charges, and that's a fair thing to note. It's also fair to note that he reportedly assisted U.S. authorities in the run-up to Maduro's capture, and that the investigation into him appears to have gone quiet around the same time. Make of that what you will. There you go, folks: doctrine, blockade, invasion, custody of the money, rewritten law, and finally a durable ownership stake. Every step both increased American leverage and moved it one degree closer to the oil itself. Three legal systems agree: this is not ok. International law The UN Charter's starting proposition, forged out of two world wars, is that states are legally equal regardless of how powerful or how badly governed they are. Article 2(4) bars the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence. The exceptions are narrow and few: a. Security Council authorization, or b. self-defense under Article 51 following an actual armed attack. There was no Security Council authorization for the attack that seized Maduro on January 3rd. There is no publicly documented Venezuelan armed attack on the United States that would trigger Article 51. A domestic criminal indictment -- leaving aside the question of its legitimacy -- gives American courts jurisdiction to put on trial someone who ends up in an American courtroom. It does not, under international law, license flying special operations forces into a foreign capital to put him there. That's not a hippie reading -- it's why the UN Secretary-General said publicly that he was "deeply concerned" the operation hadn't respected international law, and why the blockade that preceded it maps almost exactly onto the UN General Assembly's own definition of aggression, which explicitly names blockading another state's ports as one of its clearest examples. American law The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to declare war, and the War Powers Resolution says that putting U.S. forces into hostilities is supposed to reflect Congress's judgment as well as the president's. Congress never declared war on Venezuela. It never passed an authorization for the use of military force there. The operation wasn't a response to an attack on American soil or American forces. The administration's position -- that a short, decapitating strike doesn't rise to a "war" requiring prior authorization -- is a real legal theory, and presidents of both parties have leaned on versions of it before. But Congress clearly didn't think the question was settled. The Senate voted 52-47 to advance a war powers resolution days after the raid, then killed it in a 51-50 procedural vote after the White House spent a week working on two wavering Republicans, with the Vice President flown in to break the tie. The House defeated a similar measure two weeks later on a dead-even 215-215 vote that Republican leaders held open for twenty extra minutes to get one more member to the floor. Congress didn't stop it after the fact -- barely. But still: that is not the same thing as Congress authorizing it. Venezuelan law This is the part almost no one in US media has covered, and it's worth serious consideration. Venezuela's constitution has plenty to say about all of this. Article 302 reserves the petroleum industry to the state as a matter of national interest. Article 303 requires the state to retain PDVSA itself (Venezuela's state-owned oil company). Article 150 requires National Assembly approval for contracts of national public interest with foreign states -- which the Assembly has, in fact, now given. (Reasonable people may note the remarkable application of coercive pressure by external forces shaping the conditions under which that consent was granted.) But approval by whom, on whose authority? Maduro's own Supreme Tribunal ruled his removal a temporary absence, not a permanent one, and under Article 234 that framework caps a vice president's caretaker role at 90 days, extendable once by the Assembly for another 90. Rodr iguez's initial 90 days expired in early April with no public Assembly vote to extend it. The outer 180-day limit came and went by early July. No extension vote. No presidential election, though Article 233 says a permanent vacancy in a president's first four years is supposed to trigger one within 30 days. Rodriguez simply kept governing, and two months after that constitutional clock ran out, her government signed a hundred-year contract over a fifth of the nation 's oil reserves. I'm not saying the concessions are automatically void, or that Venezuelan courts and the Assembly can't retroactively bless what's happened -- they plainly intend to, and probably will, for as long as this government holds power. What I am saying is that a future, differently constituted Venezuelan government has a serious, textually grounded argument that an interim administration whose own constitutional clock had already expired -- ergo, who should no longer be serving in office, since elections were constitutionally required to be held -- lacked the authority to bind the country for a century. If you want a hundred-year oil contract, the first thing you need is a government whose legitimacy can survive more than six months. This one, on its own country's terms, currently cannot. Consent under a gun Suppose you set all three of those legal problems aside. Suppose Rodriguez's government signs, the Assembly ratifies, and Venezuelan courts eventually bless the whole structure. There's still a harder question sitting underneath the paperwork: what is consent worth when the party asking for it also controls the coercive environment the "yes" gets produced in? The 1969 Vienna Convention has a name for this. Article 52 says a treaty procured by the unlawful threat or use of force is void. I'm not claiming that single clause dissolves a three-layer commercial arrangement involving a private company and private equity terms -- it doesn't work that cleanly, and Reuters' own reporting treats the governmental agreement, the Venezuelan concessions, and the corporate equity deal as legally distinct layers. But the governmental layer is exactly the scenario the clause was written for: One state invades another, removes its government, keeps a military and economic chokehold on it, tells the world out loud that the target now needs its permission to trade -- and then negotiates a resource deal with the successor authority that situation produced, and calls the result consensual. Really now. Try the universality test, which is the single most useful tool in this whole argument: would you accept this reasoning from anyone else? Imagine China invading a mineral-rich neighbor, capturing its president, propping up his own deputy as "interim president," and then announcing a hundred-year mining concession with a Chinese government equity stake, on the grounds that the interim government approved it. Nobody serious would call that a legitimate contract. Therefore, it doesn't become one just because DC did it instead of Beijing. Interest, right, sovereignty, duty Let's break this down. There are four fundamental concepts we're working with here. (And I'm sick and tired of real and important words being turned into a funhouse mirror of meaning, just so powerful interests can do whatever they want, sabotage our clarity of mind, and keep us from fighting back because we can't even talk about things clearly. So. Definitions.) An interest is something that benefits you. America has real interests in Venezuelan oil, in keeping hostile militaries out of this hemisphere, and in a stable, diversified energy supply. A right is something you're entitled to demand. Wanting Venezuelan oil, even wanting it for excellent reasons, does not create an American right to it. Sovereignty is the principle that it's Venezuelans -- not Americans, Russians, or Chinese -- who get to decide what happens to Venezuela's resources and government, within the bounds of international law and the rights of Venezuelans themselves. And duty is what power is supposed to cost you. The more capability a state has to simply take what it wants, the less credible its excuse for just-taking-it becomes. Power is supposed to be ennobling. There's an old line, popularized of all places by a comic-book hero, that has outlived the comic: with great power comes great responsibility. It sounds almost too simple to belong in a foreign policy essay, and that's exactly why it belongs here. What I hear underneath Miller's four words, and underneath a hundred-year contract signed with a government whose own legal clock had run out, is closer to the inverse: with great power comes great impunity. "We can, therefore we may and we will, and if you don 't like it -- who's going to stop us?" That might be an accurate description of what power enables you to do. It is not a theory of law; it is definitely not a theory of moral goodness, equal dignity, or mutual respect; and it is a genuinely dangerous theory of leadership, because it only works for exactly as long as you're the strongest party in the room, and no country stays that forever. An angry man filled with lust may be capable of overpowering a woman. That does not make rape OK. The best version of their case -- and why it still isn't enough Let's steelman this: Maduro ran an authoritarian, corrupt government that stole an election and impoverished its own people. Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence in the hemisphere is a long-term security concern. Venezuela's oil industry has been starved of capital and expertise for two decades and desperately needs both. American investment could genuinely help rebuild it. If Rodriguez's government and the National Assembly want to strike this bargain, maybe that's Venezuela choosing the least-bad option available to it. I take all of that seriously. My answer is: then make that case to a government whose authority isn 't itself in dispute, and make an offer good enough that Venezuelans choose it freely. Offer the investment, the technology, the market access, the debt relief. Compete for that relationship the way you'd want a suitor to compete for something that's actually yours to give away. If getting the deal required warships, a military abduction, an economic chokehold, and a government installed by the same power now buying its resources -- that isn't evidence the deal is a good one. It's evidence that, were it offered honestly, it might not have been accepted at all. The superpower I actually want None of this is an argument for American weakness. On the contrary. It's an argument for America to be stronger , in the specific way that matters most: discipline. Integrity. Self-restraint. Responsibility. I want America to be powerful enough to keep its word. To live up to its ideals. To honor its treaties and uphold its responsibilities. To be a force for good in the world. To provide help in times of disaster, and support recovery with dignity instead of possessive self-interest. To negotiate with respect, to act with integrity, and to genuinely participate in building a better, stronger, more peaceful world, jointly with the many other people and countries with whom we share this planet. In my ideal world, America keeps sea lanes open; deters attacks on its people without attacking anyone else; secures its (green!) energy future; invests in climate justice, resilience, and adaptation; and negotiates genuinely excellent deals. It's strong enough that other countries choose to trade with it because the offer is good, not because refusing carries an economic or military price. This means America must be strong enough to exercise restraint -- because restraint only means something when you could dominate someone and choose not to. Nearly every empire in history has managed to make weaker countries obey it for a while. That was never the hard test. The hard test, the one very few powers have ever passed, is whether you can hold overwhelming power and not become a bully with it. "But Not To Us." Stephen Miller probably thought he was making a throwaway point on cable news. Read against everything that followed -- the blockade, the raid, the custody of the money, the rewritten petroleum law, the equity stake, the hundred-year lease on a fifth of a country's oil -- it reads less like a gaffe and more like the whole doctrine, stated nakedly before anyone had bothered to dress it up. Venezuela has the right to sell its oil to the United States. It has the right to sell it to China. It has the right to make a bad deal and the right to make a brilliant one. Its government has duties to its own people, and its people have rights against their government that no foreign power gets to override on their behalf. America can compete, invest, negotiate, and protect its own interests with everything it's got. What it can't do -- what no country gets to do, no matter how big its navy is -- is decide that its need for something someone else owns, makes that something rightfully its own. We tell children that with great power comes great responsibility. It might be superpowers that need the reminder most. Because the alternative -- great power, great impunity, and everyone else can shove it -- doesn't stop with Venezuela. It ends in a world where every strong state takes what it can get away with, every weak one arms itself against the possibility, and sovereignty means nothing more than whatever the strongest military in the room says it means. We built something better than that world once, out of the wreckage of two world wars. It would be a genuine shame to trade that hard-won architecture of geopolitical responsibility for 65 billion barrels. * If this kind of work is valuable to you -- the research, the fact-checking, the willingness to actually sit with the legal texts instead of just the headlines -- the best way to support it is to become a paid subscriber on Substack, . | Brave for Good Dear Friend, Will you help me put God back in your town schools? Specifically, I'm asking you to sign the "Schools Need a Bible Revival" petition and tell your Governor that the children in your community deserve to hear that: They are wonderfully ma | | | | | Dear Friend, Will you help me put God back in your town schools? Specifically, I'm asking you to sign the "[**Schools Need a Bible Revival**](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkkafvPI0eiPW8uUlNqApy-B8NPfwKfrB0p0oECPSeuXJxM-80YAvLlkuMAkjaTDOQskIUpJDmJm-1iVxn5ondOXEBh4ksVgL9F)" petition and tell your Governor that the children in your community deserve to hear that: They are wonderfully made in the very image of God. And that God is calling them to love Him above all else. What a country we'd be, if all of America's children had just a little bit of God's Word in their lives - like you did. But in 1963, in a wrongly decided Supreme Court case, the Left ripped the everyday reading of the Bible out of public schools. **And the results speak for themselves: more violence, divorce, abortion, drug addiction, depression, and the breakdown of the family.** It is only fitting that during the 250th Anniversary of our independence, we put Biblical lessons BACK into our public schools. **[That's why I'm spearheading a nationwide Bible Revival in public schools and asking you to join me today. ](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDklDzwfZ0tQIgjVqu2ItWdAcTzytJMxAcIkUVYVK5m0FSviA-pz06XXEoNpg6fyqluV752KkxAjwcwWLwzvV7IMlXeXZYP8BB9n)** Your signature on your "[**Schools Need a Bible Revival**](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkmYCz5sUbbQ7BUElfjXRD7J_fTizc1OWsLvC6JEawtWQUD8Zzd5dNHRme30TepnJ2S9EIJSTv_b0cUmMJZC6bEtGJZtmnszt88)" petition tells our representatives that you want biblical lessons put back in schools. Your signed "**[Schools Need a Bible Revival](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDknazWqlQCQ9MGPXi1nXaHt1_9cx6g9aS7FU6cw6UUnWlShqI86xEgOfaxKM3nfJXlQaRCI24UmqRYknMA1thFsSQaGTADcEDCd)** " petition is going straight to my friends at **BRAVE FOR GOOD**. **BRAVE FOR GOOD** is the powerhouse group behind my "See You at the Library" movement featured on Fox News, that gets conservative Story Hours into public libraries to counter the Left's "Drag Queen Story Hours." **BRAVE FOR GOOD** is the powerhouse group that got an historic conservative Story Hour into the Library of Congress last year! And **BRAVE FOR GOOD** is the powerhouse group that will get the Biblical values you cherish - and that America was founded upon - **back into public schools this year!** HOW? We've designed a mini-curriculum for America's 250th Anniversary that teaches children about the role of the Bible in our nation's Founding and emphasizes the Founding values that have made our country great. Last year I got into three public schools to reach 1,400 children with biblical lessons. **[With you and BRAVE FOR GOOD behind me, I know we can expand that number to 250,000 children this year in honor of America's 250th Anniversary. ](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkocCDS4os3ERB9tLnAuW4JfWrIHGAkq9TypQbODeejsjPZdHnXMFZAXzbNgBmZFj4D94Czxnlw07CBnCcIRc1I6yKcE-7wnRGg)** That's why **BRAVE FOR GOOD** is getting ready for the battle by collecting stacks of petitions. Your signed "**[Schools Need a Bible Revival](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkpqCwbHgsDj-_PzgmR2k0KjTm3GbuxvE9s84JUOL9jIelc4zKRluZOpGe0Xb20YtY7pbWSUGdHDnPdllXd1cOSWJ0mORi0Fxeg)** " petition tells our representatives that the Supreme Court ruling that took the Bible out of schools only specified that the Bible could not be mandatory reading. The 1963 ruling 100% allows for the Bible to be taught in a historical or cultural context! And why wouldn’t it be? In every corner of the world, the Bible is considered one of the greatest books ever written. Of course children should learn about it in your taxpayer-funded schools! But radical educators will try to keep anything to do with the Bible out of our schools and when they do, **BRAVE FOR GOOD** will be ready to counter them with thousands of signed petitions. **[But that means getting your signed "Schools Need a Bible Revival" petition back now. And will you please also consider a tax-deductible petition sponsorship gift of $35 or more? ](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkqoYRlGRvj5BdWcIZf1Pl3Dfclw7hiX2dZZFn7oeOr870wrqFmES6t5zBF4gW8p2XrE-BLRUrGFgXs2NPouZpkxehagG-mZS38)** Every petition you send digitally must still be delivered, verified, securely collected, and tabulated before it can be presented - and **[your $35 covers those costs for 400 more signers.](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ5OTF9AAwAAAAAAsnibDkr1HvlbOujdlU3jmNAWzR-g0PI9ifrTKEkJQG3xcLrBZirmmR-WO_theqLkP_1sMkcLvasr8In872lNV_CJVX_LgBTo3-qawGQ) **That means your gift today puts hundreds of new voices on the record before the deadline. Together with **BRAVE FOR GOOD** and patriots like you, we got conservative and patriotic values back into public libraries. _Now we're going to get biblical values back into public schools. _ Only God can lead our nation back to His Word. **But you and I are called to do our part too.** Thank you for standing with us. May God bless you,

Peter,
The state of Texas suspended 1.2 million voters ahead of the November midterm elections.
That equates to about 6% of all Texas voters, more than enough to swing a close race in the state. That is exactly the kind of margin that could be catastrophic for Democrats, with polls showing Democrat James Talarico virtually tied with GOP candidate Ken Paxton in a hotly contested Senate race that could decide control of the chamber.
Texas voters have until October 5th to check and update their voter registration if they are impacted. They can check their voter registration status by visiting the [Texas secretary of state's website](https://yfq78zhbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=0017Jiwb-9Cm3Cxog4PgyKXiBmT7vOagfZCIVZP3Nw0kdSI97kweLx2zMife9szdnZ_k0Snwn1ADrldO8K5ObcJ5LaKUoAWk8w0C3LmyoPsIc6BSli5GtbFvOp38QsA-LWdvDehCsexVJTRU8mKeZ8ierHlZr1m5zIfBq3pTxs_NoPpV1vz8hZr3I8RNWRJ0ZeQG_yV-yDcpEYog31651pQ8A==&c=T0s-9lSNZiUyAUFBR_LxsT-mZGTU0zzESarU6WVaGno5QtoHfAzntQ==&ch=9LK9EIIkDLAkLuE1xg37BgFLxqMFPYj1W5nD6pk_4krhhqLFhMk3Og==) or by visiting their county election office.
If voters don't update their voter registration in time, they can still vote but it will be more difficult. Voters who show up to the polls with a suspended voter registration must complete a "statement of residence" form, and anyone who has moved to a different county will either have to vote in their previous one or cast a provisional ballot instead.

**Good Morning!** On this day in 1901, at the Pan-American Exhibition in Buffalo, [President William McKinley](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGupCAUxvGnwQ6DRxa1oNjGbrbd0gAex7MLaOBkjG9_M5P7Brf-JV--_P8-loejSPn5xyW0vB1LxqtGZMayJFoZS_KOOWKlzJgrbTfvCygwUk1SmcUFphcu2jWr3RAB-wZtN4yjGadu1M1uw9YB6mkE74chIGzeh34woF3QnVFdQ_a9pyZlOqUM9O2keudV-GXW4HW_jUIrXImP0v47KPOOW7yPF5Y2HKmJdmc-q-h_C5gFzNd1tTtVPsr9dgEz71Tl6m5JWX6LgLniyZg8FmkEzGfBSitmlhfFSC7JFP5TjnhLqrLuBzfFrucHqxmEVs_kKH4e8A_DvSx8BQAA__9XlYYe) was shot twice in the chest by 28-year-old anarchist Leon Czolgosz. As he fell, he said, "_Be careful how you tell my wife_." Music lovers may remember Columbia House ads promising a dozen albums for a penny--never mind the required future purchases. As we read in today's [_Whatever Happened To ..._](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGupDAQBNDTQOaRMayBwMEmZLPphqhtt4fetTGyG0Zz-y_-FX5USempVH-f6xMo0v76AwkNh7zu-K4RmbGsiTxjSRaYI1baGfdK4cPbqqTSQs5C6hUc04XrAK03AVFh36LpxmnS09xNQ7uZ3oYOfCedldapUc-jmpyEPgSvlR18S-b25Cx1J6VW_WOWPVjpfmnv7NCHqRkkeuJcHv8y7bxhiJ98YXm4nNpoNuajNv3vRi2NWlwk9x8SFnKww11p1JLQE9x5VnKNWnL0IgFFkYvHIgq6XLxw8bRVODiIcxQuxzNZAnHR_okCoj1TFQwH1rYYf7wpRqp6bAb5uq3vNfzDEy-jvgIAAP__ALmK1w), the mail-order club that once boasted more than 16 million members will close shop next week. In case you missed it, this week on _The Flyover Podcast,_ Ayla counted down the seven purchases experts say you need to make before you retire. Research shows these are the buys worth making while the paychecks are still coming in, and some are pricier than you'd think. Ayla ranked all seven by urgency, and the one at the top of the list only gets more expensive the longer you wait. ## Legal Battles Shape Midterms
The Trump administration [_will appeal a decision_](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuwyAURb8Gb0QYbIwHhkqVt1TdOlrYPOKXYojgJWn-vnJ_ofPVvbrnfJ3ns8OI6fLhdrAU8pzgWSMQQZl39ARlXxxRhIqJIFUML9pmKaTmYuRCz24lfMDcucbbACBBNWDbwRhtxtZ0zWY7MIMcFtf2owjBu84opeRgtGpHP3jfoD32xCh0K4SW6jQK5Rax9tqvS6eCYZ0Aj5TL6Zox0QYhvvIDymnNexPtRnSrTL0xOTE5uWU9GI6MyekzRyRcK5NTAA_FRX69-wtw-CFIvvIl5vWbJ3jye71VvjuMfHExZmJyqpTLi6kJPVPvrdKy7UVvmmL97YkxYtUD68TlKP19oX8qfFj5GwAA__8Cooal) made by a federal judge that prohibits the U.S. Postal Service from implementing an executive order seeking to limit mail voting during the midterms. In a busy day of court decisions, the Supreme Court also ruled that [_party committees paying for TV advertisements_](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGO5CAQRL8GZ4wYzNgQEFzibC-90MJNe917GCxoj7V_f_L9wsalKtV7fz7mj0CJ8ufvsKPntcwZr5aQGeu8U2Ss-xKYEzbKjLnR-s3brJUepHJSDXMApjfOJnTRr4ga-w79c7R2sO5pTbd547TRi4JXgKice9q4GmVhxMWNTlvdkb_3lFPDU6lB9w-n-nAXhgiL6VcrjMJIXOrjq1DmDdf0Xd5YH1D2LvmN-Wii_yX0JPR0XdcjL3Bz3LnQ01ESMUETemrnUXFHCeWsLPT0dTYmwCaXAH9lxeNcEkHITWJCYCpZhihrYJSR2nEyylwBZK4N5AogK-Twcq9Xb7vq43FRStSGURj1uQdK_x_yD8W-vf4XAAD__zmbkNQ) can take advantage of the same discounts that candidates get, allowing the well-funded Republican National Committee to stretch its dollars further. **Whatever happened to Columbia House Records?** If you grew up in the 1960s, '70s, or '80s, you probably remember the ritual: flipping to the back of your favorite magazine, [finding that Columbia House ad](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGupDAQBNDTQOaRMayBwMEmZLPphqhtt4fetTGyG0Zz-y_-FX5USempVH-f6xMo0v76AwkNh7zu-K4RmbGsiTxjSRaYI1baGfdK4cPbqqTSQs5C6hUc04XrAK03AVFh36LpxmnS09xNQ7uZ3oYOfCedldapUc-jmpyEPgSvlR18S-b25Cx1J6VW_WOWPVjpfmnv7NCHqRkkeuJcHv8y7bxhiJ98YXm4nNpoNuajNv3vRi2NWlwk9x8SFnKww11p1JLQE9x5VnKNWnL0IgFFkYvHIgq6XLxw8bRVODiIcxQuxzNZAnHR_okCoj1TFQwH1rYYf7wpRqp6bAb5uq3vNfzDEy-jvgIAAP__ALmK1w), and agonizing over which 12 albums to claim for a single penny.

For millions of young music lovers, especially kids in small towns without a record store, it felt like a miracle. You didn't need a credit card. You didn't need to be 18. You just taped a penny to a piece of cardboard, mailed it to Terre Haute, Indiana, and waited for a box of records to change your life. Columbia Records launched the mail-order club in 1955 to reach rural and suburban listeners. It rebranded as Columbia House in the early '70s and became a cultural juggernaut, peaking in 1996 with 16 million members and $1.4 billion in annual revenue. At one point, it was one of the biggest music retailers in America. But the penny was never really a penny. The deal required you to buy [more albums at full price](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGOqzAQgOHTmI5osB1jChevoctrt0SDPYRZGRzhSSJuv8peYftfX_F_3aYbcub9_h83CrKUaad3zSRCx7RxEjq2GUUyVd6F9srLKeukQbsWhhbchFH4RZPFJoWFSJNpKHS9984PnbfNGpa-94PtZoTokut68GisS2i8vUa01HD4eDCA6wCcNpcBDM4Qry7F2ZrFKwuUWMpx-S68y0pLPsuLjkssW5PDKvKoyvxTelR6lCKY8ykreaifQukxlvzcZsZ2Lc9KreCDqtJjc4T0eHPOXF2vLNw35PyLyh9fvIL-CQAA__-TzXSe)--and if you forgot to mail back that monthly rejection card, a record you never asked for showed up with a bill.

Kids nationwide learned to game the system: signing up under fake names, writing "Return to Sender" on unwanted shipments, or pleading that they were minors who couldn't legally be held to a contract. The collection letters became a generational punch line. Then came Napster, iTunes, and Spotify. By 2014, revenues had collapsed to just $17 million. Columbia House filed for bankruptcy in 2015 and limped along as an obscure online DVD catalog. Next week, on Sept. 15, the lights go out for good, ending a 71-year run. Somewhere, a 72-year-old is wondering if they still owe for that Engelbert Humperdinck album. _Did you buy records or tapes for a penny from Columbia House? Did you ever fulfill your contract? Let us know your thoughts by replying to this email._

If you grew up in the 1960s, '70s, or '80s, you probably remember the ritual: flipping to the back of your favorite magazine, , and agonizing over which 12 albums to claim for a single penny. For millions of young music lovers, especially kids in small towns without a record store, it felt like a miracle. You didn't need a credit card. You didn't need to be 18. You just taped a penny to a piece of cardboard, mailed it to Terre Haute, Indiana, and waited for a box of records to change your life. Columbia Records launched the mail-order club in 1955 to reach rural and suburban listeners. It rebranded as Columbia House in the early '70s and became a cultural juggernaut, peaking in 1996 with 16 million members and $1.4 billion in annual revenue. At one point, it was one of the biggest music retailers in America. But the penny was never really a penny. The deal required you to buy if you forgot to mail back that monthly rejection card, a record you never asked for showed up with a bill. Kids nationwide learned to game the system: signing up under fake names, writing "Return to Sender" on unwanted shipments, or pleading that they were minors who couldn't legally be held to a contract. The collection letters became a generational punch line. Then came Napster, iTunes, and Spotify. By 2014, revenues had collapsed to just $17 million. Columbia House filed for bankruptcy in 2015 and limped along as an obscure online DVD catalog. Next week, on Sept. 15, the lights go out for good, ending a 71-year run. Christian parents and grandparents across America will walk into their local public libraries with their children and grandchildren.And in a matter of hours, hundreds of Story Hours will fill children's hearts with goodness, gratitude, and God.This is our chance to bring God's truth into libraries across America and reach an entire generation of children. **This year, honoring America's 250th birthday, our ambitious goal is to expand "See You at the Library Day" to reach 250,000 children.****And we are just ONE MONTH away.** Before then, I need you!The response from parents, grandparents, and patriots who want to host "Story Hours" has been overwhelming.But it's going to be a big undertaking and expensive to give these volunteers the resources they need to hold "Story Hours" for 250,000 children.**And with just over one month left, the clock is running out to fund the Story Hours we need to reach 250,000 children.** **[That's why I'm asking you to rush back your tax-deductible sponsorship gift of $35, $50, $125, $250 or more today.](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyUkc1u2zoQhZ-G2tHgXyhqoYUDW8EF4tvCNVJ0RQzJkU1UIgWKctC3LxwkD9DtwTcz-Ob8PNkTxCmm6_8wY1_qaMtq3zGn6c8N7pgTzjnVmxVMaMo6yrQFX-MdrYIm9MEH4L7BnrfG6I5ppZpbb1hoPR-ZCEqDk9KgEs6MTjpmOua6JvaPfaxjmjPJlNwxwFaic6MP4DBoohhMWOqu4LK5KXpIFdbfYy4edz7PzdTfal1WIvdEDEQMK_qt4A4ShlwfBBGDK3BHOuZCrzkHIoYFmOFylMFQJ5FTxUVHjQuGguy60D4Fyf0TkcNWZ7vmrXgk8nA-vhGhH9GMIW4zkYfjaf_f62foYV4gXhORh08pbp8PL_Z5ePlmz8c3-wHbH7_2l1d-ot_39HwZvmZzqpjq48hloF8_aUoflvc4TXHVLVHsOkOcPqzrvzZ078XfAAAA__8Wm5mI)** Friend, America's children need to hear our message because today's "educators" and librarians are radicals! Back when you were growing up, you may remember lazy Saturdays at the library with a kind but stern librarian.She would fill your mind with classics like Pat the Bunny and The Little Engine That Could.But today, all that has changed. Instead of filling children with wholesome stories, radical activists have worked to turn our public libraries into vehicles for their values.But we can't just sit back and complain about it. **[That's why parents and grandparents across the country are rising up through "See You at the Library Day."](https://email.alert.republicantaskforce.com/c/eJyUkc1u2zoQhZ-G2tHgXyhqoYUDW8EF4tvCNVJ0RQzJkU1UIgWKctC3LxwkD9DtwTcz-Ob8PNkTxCmm6_8wY1_qaMtq3zGn6c8N7pgTzjnVmxVMaMo6yrQFX-MdrYIm9MEH4L7BnrfG6I5ppZpbb1hoPR-ZCEqDk9KgEs6MTjpmOua6JvaPfaxjmjPJlNwxwFaic6MP4DBoohhMWOqu4LK5KXpIFdbfYy4edz7PzdTfal1WIvdEDEQMK_qt4A4ShlwfBBGDK3BHOuZCrzkHIoYFmOFylMFQJ5FTxUVHjQuGguy60D4Fyf0TkcNWZ7vmrXgk8nA-vhGhH9GMIW4zkYfjaf_f62foYV4gXhORh08pbp8PL_Z5ePlmz8c3-wHbH7_2l1d-ot_39HwZvmZzqpjq48hloF8_aUoflvc4TXHVLVHsOkOcPqzrvzZ078XfAAAA__8Wm5mI)** We're countering those awful "Drag Queen Story Hours" with conservative Story Hours filled with the classic books you and I grew up with, plus new wholesome books that captivate children with lessons in bravery, honesty, kindness, and patriotism.And on October 3, a little boy or girl will stand up at their public library as straight and tall as they possibly can... ...as their right hand covers their heart, and they proudly pledge allegiance to our American flag.We'll teach them:**Freedom Requires Courage.****Great Blessings Require Great Sacrifice.****IN GOD WE TRUST.** And we hope to engrave those lessons on every child's heart at "See You at the Library Day."But first, we have to get the resources into the hands of the parents, grandparents, and patriots who are organizing these Story Hours.Your tax-deductible sponsorship gift helps send a "Story Hour Kit" to volunteers organizing "See You at the Library" events. Christian parents and grandparents across America will walk into their local public libraries with their children and grandchildren.And in a matter of hours, hundreds of Story Hours will fill children's hearts with goodness, gratitude, and God.This is our chance to bring God's truth into libraries across America and reach an entire generation of children. This year, honoring America's 250th birthday, our ambitious goal is to expand "See You at the Library Day" to reach 250,000 children.And we are just ONE MONTH away. Before then, I need you!The response from parents, grandparents, and patriots who want to host "Story Hours" has been overwhelming.But it's going to be a big undertaking and expensive to give these volunteers the resources they need to hold "Story Hours" for 250,000 children.And with just over one month left, the clock is running out to fund the Story Hours we need to reach 250,000 children. Friend, America's children need to hear our message because today's "educators" and librarians are radicals! Back when you were growing up, you may remember lazy Saturdays at the library with a kind but stern librarian.She would fill your mind with classics like Pat the Bunny and The Little Engine That Could.But today, all that has changed. Instead of filling children with wholesome stories, radical activists have worked to turn our public libraries into vehicles for their values.But we can't just sit back and complain about it. We're countering those awful "Drag Queen Story Hours" with conservative Story Hours filled with the classic books you and I grew up with, plus new wholesome books that captivate children with lessons in bravery, honesty, kindness, and patriotism.And on October 3, a little boy or girl will stand up at their public library as straight and tall as they possibly can... ...as their right hand covers their heart, and they proudly pledge allegiance to our American flag.We'll teach them:Freedom Requires Courage.Great Blessings Require Great Sacrifice.IN GOD WE TRUST. ## Education Board Finalizes Social Studies Rewrite
The State Board of Education gave final approval Friday to high school social studies standards requiring students to learn that the Sept. 11 attacks were motivated by ["radical Islam"](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGOpDAQRU8DmZExxrQDB5uQ9aYbonK5aCwZjGwDvbcf0RppDjDZC6q-_n__ntMTfPDb6y-sZMp7jtNGVw5UCqUJj5Q8HuFYcYHtRdnRmkvEOAkuFOOacTUBFn_SJKF2xnKn25pMOzweSote6XoxOOCj73vlet32FoTuLGDHJUmN2na29uaO45qrtuVCDk0vFCds5wGEHGzLK8nJ-RJTUxYq9IY8h__xpNRgXOtgllL2XHV_KjFWYryuq5njW95D7oNKjDdWYvy8MnIHQvFxYzZCcgz2PcWTMsO4lZtS9hBYxiXGwH4csG8JdTJuv3wIPquhkvy1gg-fJuW3Bk8jvgIAAP__hfuKXA). That wording replaces a narrower focus on the terrorist groups behind the attacks. Lessons also present the Prophet Muhammad as a warrior who spread the faith through violence and slavery. The Republican majority [approved each section](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkMGupCAQRb9GdxioVmkWLGbTuzfbWZoCCiVBMVDab_5-8voXZntzc3Jy_nwtX5hyOtbfuJPl71iWg94tEzPVxV-1Jn_la_cbHiu1QHvj4ssCEmYhjZDzgp7TTcuIfbBOBqN6sko_n7OBaTb9Zp9uUqAfClArdBOQMRCj0xAe0cig-2R_cNLIWSkJox4mmCV5FTXCqJ2S3SgpJC514I2YvrHF_LfcVAdf9j7bjfls3eNXB68OXs0VGj6vYS33z8DIJFzBGkSJgsLlkVM5OniNYmvCl6s2auKdeBO-RCfwPGu5KQjc6Qg7HdyGM8S-2nC-U86pzbob5bpjyh8H_t92t4V_AQAA__9dtoaH) after testimony that ran mostly against it. Member Julie Pickren, who backed the changes, said the vote "bookends 12 years of life's work." Muslim speakers had asked members to restore a deleted standard on Muslim contributions to algebra and astronomy. The advocacy group CAIR says it will work to overturn the standards, which reach classrooms in 2030.

name: Chris Deluzio
subject: My decision
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Deluzio for Congress
body:
At 17 years old, I first raised my right hand and swore an oath to our Constitution.
# [](https://act.chrisforpa.com/go/46?t=1&akid=83%2E42639%2EGR1pZU)
[](https://act.chrisforpa.com/go/28?c0=deluzio-em-26-q3.tyfWFC&refcode=em260906&refcode2=83.42639.GR1pZU&t=2&akid=83%2E42639%2EGR1pZU)
---
At 17 years old, I first raised my right hand and swore an oath to our Constitution. After the 9/11 attacks during my senior year of high school, I went off to the Naval Academy.
I still remember walking into Memorial Hall. It's where we honor all alumni who have died in service to our country.
I was commissioned as an active-duty surface warfare officer in the U.S. Navy, and went on to serve at sea and then on the ground with a U.S. Army Civil Affairs unit in Iraq.
I first decided to run for Congress in 2021 because my time in uniform shaped me considerably. That is where I learned the power of solidarity, that we don't leave people behind, and that it doesn't matter your class, your race, who you love or what you look like or where you're from – that we are all in this together.
I looked around and didn't see a lot of leaders, especially on the right, who saw the world that way. I saw too many more interested in serving the most powerful corporations and the billionaires who bankroll them.
We won that election and then won again in 2024, a year Trump won in PA.
Today, I'm running for reelection because patriotism demands courage in this moment. The courage to fight for our freedom. The courage to fight the corruption and abuses of the Trump administration. The courage to fight to restore the American dream — a dream that's no longer real, or never was for many. It's been ripped away by powerful corporations and the corruption of concentrated power.
Western PA sent a fighter to Washington. And I am not done.
But I can't win reelection alone. I need you in this fight with me, especially as the last Democrat in Pennsylvania who represents a battleground seat.
So I am asking:
**[Can you please make a contribution to my reelection campaign today? Our average online donation is around $30. Many give more. Some give less. No amount is too small. It will all add up fast when so many are giving what they can.](https://act.chrisforpa.com/go/28?c0=deluzio-em-26-q3.tyfWFC&refcode=em260906&t=3&akid=83%2E42639%2EGR1pZU)**

Hey, it’s Congressman Johnny Olszewski. Apologies for the early morning message (especially on a holiday weekend). That saying is more true than you could ever imagine.** Here’s what I mean: Every grassroots donation we bring in today stretches a whole lot further than a donation we receive the day before the election. Trust me, your donation today is worth more than a donation ten times that amount in November!**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/138660469/644799157/1153820233?refcode=email_090626_early&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDcvMS8xMDU4MjciLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiYmIxNjNhZWQtZWNhOS1mMTExLTliMzMtMDAyMjQ4MmE5MzNiIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=IZNhYFHexFYTquqzvMUf9Q8xf3ck4RWS_ltPG_x_-0k=) It makes sense, right? A major regulatory shift has quietly taken effect across American retirement accounts in 2026.

Under SECURE 2.0 (Section 603), the IRS has officially activated mandatory Roth rules for catch-up contributions. At the same time, lawmakers in Washington have introduced legislation targeting high-balance IRAs and 401(k)s with mandatory withdrawals and contribution limits.

With over $47.6 trillion currently sitting in U.S. retirement assets, Washington is aggressively shifting rules to collect tax revenue immediately rather than waiting for future payouts.

Renowned retirement expert Bob Carlson - who has tracked Capitol Hill tax policy for over 35 years - warns that most retirees are completely unprepared for how these changes will impact tax liabilities.

For anyone holding assets in a 401(k), Traditional IRA, or Roth IRA, reviewing your strategy today is critical.
